newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warns Israel company about Cuba investments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns Israel company about Cuba investments.

text.p: The United States has warned an Israeli company that its business deals in Cuba might be in violation of the Helms-Burton law, a senior U.S. official said on Friday.
Commerce undersecretary Stuart Eizenstat named the company as the BM Group and said it was involved in sugar and citrus production in the communist-ruled Caribbean island.

"A dozen (companies) more are being investigated, and only in the past few days an advisory letter has been sent out (to the BM Group), which we believe may be in violation of the act," Eizenstat said at a news conference.

The United States last year imposed sanctions on Canadian mining firm Sherritt International and Mexico's Grupo Domos telecommunications concern under the Helms-Burton law, which punishes foreign companies that invest in property confiscated from U.S. citizens in Cuba.

Under that legislation, the United States must deny entry to top executives and main stockholders of firms found to be "trafficking" with disputed Cuban properties. The same punishment is extended to their spouses and minor children.

The law, which toughened Washington's 35-year-old embargo against Cuba, was enacted in March shortly after the Cuban air force shot down two small U.S. civilian aircraft over the Florida Straits, killing four men from Miami.
Eizenstat said that around 12 other foreign companies had either stopped using U.S. confiscated property in Cuba or had dropped investment plans in the island due to the legislation.
As an example he cited Mexican cement giant Cemex SA, which had been eyeing a deal with the Cuban government to run a portlant plant formerly owned by a U.S. company.
The United States, however, has refrained from putting into effect another part of the Helms-Burton law that would allow U.S. citizens to sue foreigners exploiting their old properties in Cuba.

President Bill Clinton announced on Friday that he was suspending for six months more the right to file suit under Helms-Burton, citing the progress achieved by the United States in drumming up international pressure against Cuba's government.
Cuban President Fidel Castro nationalised the properties of some 5,900 U.S. companies and individuals after taking power in a 1959 revolution.
